passage:
At Amara's flat in London, Nadia watched Amara's mother arrive from Lagos with three coolers of food. By the second evening, Mrs. Okafor had filled Amara's plate with jollof rice four times. When Amara said, 'Mummy, I'm full,' her mother's smile fell. 'You don't like my cooking anymore?' She turned back to the stove, shoulders stiff.
Nadia saw Amara pause, then go over and hug her mother from behind. 'I love it so much I want it for breakfast too. Pack me some for tomorrow?'
Her mother laughed and took the plate. Nadia, whose own mother did the same with parathas, understood. The food was never really about hunger.

qa.q: Where had Amara's mother come from?
qa.a: From Lagos.

qa.q: What did Nadia feel watching this, and why?
qa.a: Nadia felt understanding and fondness, recognising her own mother's parathas in Mrs. Okafor's jollof rice.

qa.q: What made Amara's second reply work?
qa.a: Amara hugged her mother, praised the food and asked for some for breakfast, accepting the love without eating past fullness.

qa.q: How did Mrs. Okafor seem to take Amara's first 'I'm full'?
qa.a: She seemed hurt and rejected, as if Amara no longer liked her cooking, which is why her smile fell and her shoulders stiffened.

grounding: Shows an observer who sees that a mother's piling of food is her language of love, and a kind response that thanks her warmly instead of simply refusing.

passage:
On visiting Sunday at the working women's hostel in Pune, Sarita watched her roommate Kiran's Amma unpack a steel tiffin carrier in the common room. Roti after roti landed on Kiran's plate.
'Amma, enough, three is plenty.'
Amma's hand froze in the air, the fourth roti hanging. 'You don't want my food now?'
Kiran took a breath, took the roti, and broke it in half. 'I'll eat this half now and the rest at dinner, so I can think of you tonight.'
Amma's face softened. Sarita noticed she still tucked two more rotis into Kiran's cupboard before leaving.

qa.q: How many rotis did Kiran say were plenty?
qa.a: Three is plenty.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt watching Amma tuck extra rotis into the cupboard?
qa.a: Sarita likely felt amused and touched, seeing how Amma's love kept finding a way through food.

qa.q: What was kind about Kiran's response?
qa.a: Kiran accepted the roti, ate a little and explained warmly that the rest would help Kiran think of Amma, so the love was received.

qa.q: How did Amma seem to feel when Kiran said 'enough'?
qa.a: Amma seemed hurt and worried, taking the refusal as a rejection of her love, which is why her hand froze.

grounding: Illustrates an observer seeing a mother keep piling roti on a plate and take refusal as rejection, and a warm response that accepts a little and explains kindly.

passage:
Dear Biji,

Thank you for the weekend in Jalandhar. I'm writing because of Sunday lunch.

You kept putting rotis on my plate, and at the fourth I put my hand over it and said, "Bas, Biji." I saw your face drop for a second, and you went quietly back to the tawa. Baljeet told me later you'd asked him whether I didn't like your cooking.

I was so sorry. I understand now: every roti was your way of saying welcome. In my family in Mangalore, love comes as endless questions; in yours, it comes hot off the tawa.

So let me say it in words: your makki roti was the best thing I've eaten this year. I stopped at three only because I was full. Next time I'll come hungry, have one more, and then ask you to teach me.

With love,
Chandrika

qa.q: What did Chandrika say at the fourth roti?
qa.a: Chandrika put a hand over the plate and said, "Bas, Biji."

qa.q: What did Chandrika feel on learning Biji thought the cooking wasn't liked?
qa.a: Chandrika felt sorry and touched, realising every roti had been Biji's way of saying welcome.

qa.q: What makes Chandrika's letter a kind response?
qa.a: It thanks Biji warmly, explains that stopping meant being full rather than disliking the food, and promises to eat one more and learn the recipe.

qa.q: How might Biji feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Biji would likely feel relieved and appreciated, her love understood even though a roti was refused.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing that a mother's endless rotis are her language of love, and answering with warm thanks and explanation.

passage:
So you asked how Dev's first lunch at my parents' went. I'm Ankita, and I have never watched anyone eat so nervously.

My mother, Vasudha, had cooked for two days. She kept sliding pooris onto his plate, one after another, and Dev kept saying, "No, Aunty, really, I'm full," in his polite way. By the sixth no, her smile had gone stiff. She went into the kitchen and banged a vessel.

I followed Dev to the balcony and explained. "In our house, food is how she says she likes you. When you refuse, she hears that you don't like her."

He looked horrified. He went straight back in, took one more poori, and said, "Aunty, this is the best aloo I've ever had. Can I take some home? I can't eat another bite now, but I don't want to miss it."

She packed him a tiffin big enough for a week. That's how I knew he was in.

qa.q: How long had Vasudha cooked for the lunch?
qa.a: Vasudha had cooked for two days.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as the refusals piled up?
qa.a: Ankita felt uneasy watching her mother's smile go stiff, understanding that each refusal sounded like rejection to her.

qa.q: How did Dev's second response work?
qa.a: He took one more, praised the aloo specifically and asked to take some home, so his refusal came wrapped in thanks.

qa.q: What did Dev's repeated 'No, Aunty' feel like to Vasudha?
qa.a: It felt like rejection; her smile went stiff and she banged a vessel in the kitchen.

grounding: Shows a young adult seeing that her mother's refilled plates are her language of love, and helping a guest respond with thanks.

passage:
I was staying at my cousin Gopika's house in Palakkad the week her new husband, Hemant, came for his first Onam there, so I saw the whole sadya battle.

Periamma served him first, then served him again before he'd swallowed. Avial, more rice, a third payasam. Hemant, who eats like a bird, kept saying, "Enough, enough," and covering the leaf with his hand.

Periamma's face fell each time. She stopped talking and started wiping the same spot on the counter.

Gopika saw it too. She leaned over and said something quietly to Hemant. Then she took Periamma's hand. "Amma, he's full up to here. He says your pal payasam is better than his mother's. Don't tell her."

Periamma laughed, a real laugh. Hemant took one more small spoon of payasam, eyes closed as if it were heaven.

I can't say what Periamma felt. But she packed him payasam for the train.

qa.q: What did Periamma pack for Hemant?
qa.a: She packed him payasam for the train.

qa.q: What does Gopika's quick move suggest she felt when she saw Periamma's face fall?
qa.a: Gopika felt concerned for her mother, understanding that each refusal felt like rejection, and wanted to soothe both sides.

qa.q: Why did Gopika's words and Hemant's extra spoon help?
qa.a: Gopika explained warmly that he was full and praised the payasam, and Hemant's one more spoon showed thanks, so the love was received, not refused.

qa.q: What was it like for Periamma each time Hemant covered the leaf?
qa.a: It felt like rejection; her face fell and she kept wiping the same spot on the counter.

grounding: Shows observers seeing that a mother's endless serving is her language of love, and a daughter helping a guest answer with warmth.

passage:
Friday: Usha, twenty-four, stayed at her friend Bhavna's house in Rajkot. At dinner, Bhavna's mother dropped roti after roti on their plates, hot from the tawa. Bhavna covered her plate. "Mummy, enough!" Her mother's face fell. She turned back to the stove, stirring hard.
Saturday: The same thing. Usha watched her face each time Bhavna refused. It wasn't pride; it looked like hurt. She noticed how early aunty had woken to knead dough, how she asked what each of them liked.
Sunday: When aunty came with another roti, Usha smiled up at her. "Aunty, your rotis are softer than my mother's. I'll take half, with ghee, and then I'm truly full." Aunty glowed and tore one carefully. Bhavna watched, then said, "Mummy, half for me too. Thank you." Her mother touched Bhavna's hair on the way back to the stove.

qa.q: What did Bhavna do when her mother dropped more roti on Friday?
qa.a: She covered her plate and said, "Mummy, enough!"

qa.q: What did Usha feel as she watched Bhavna's mother on Saturday?
qa.a: Usha felt tender and thoughtful, realising the mother's face showed hurt, and that feeding was her way of showing love.

qa.q: What made Usha's response kind?
qa.a: She thanked aunty warmly, praised the rotis and took a little more before explaining she was full, which honoured the love behind the food.

qa.q: How does Bhavna's mother experience refusals of her roti?
qa.a: She feels them as rejection, turning away and stirring hard, because feeding is how she shows love.

grounding: It illustrates an observer who sees that a mother's extra rotis are her language of love and responds with thanks and warm explanation.
